content.title: Osman Kavala case: Human Rights Court condemns Turkey
content.lead: More than seven years ago, the Strasbourg court demanded the release of Turkish cultural patron Kavala. Now the court finds further human rights violations.

image.author: Reuters
image.caption: Kavala has been imprisoned since 2017.
image.altText: Turkish philanthropist Osman Kavala, jailed since 2017 on a charge of seeking to overthrow the government, is seen at an unspecified area in this undated handout photo received by Reuters, October 26, 2021. Anadolu Culture Center/Handout via REUTERS. ATTENTION EDITORS - THIS IMAGE HAS BEEN SUPPLLIED BY A THIRD PARTY. NO SALES. NO ARCHIVES. MANDATORY CREDIT

content.text: (dpa) The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) condemned Turkey over the criminal proceedings and detention of Turkish intellectual Osman Kavala. The Strasbourg judges concluded that the country wanted to silence Kavala and demanded the activist's immediate release due to serious human rights violations.

His conviction was therefore to be considered invalid, the court said. It added that, among other things, Kavala's right to a fair trial had been violated, and in this case, there were justified doubts about the independence of the Turkish courts.

Kavala has been held in Silivri high-security prison since 2017 and was sentenced in April 2022 to life imprisonment for attempting to overthrow the government in connection with the anti-government Gezi protests in 2013. The verdict provoked sharp international criticism.

The judges found that the human rights activist had merely exercised his right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. These very rights had not been respected due to an arbitrary interpretation of a Turkish law and the resulting conviction.
According to the ECHR, Turkey also violates the prohibition of inhuman treatment, as Kavala has no real prospect of release or a legal review of his life sentence.

Already in a December 2019 ruling, the Strasbourg court had found human rights violations and at that time demanded Kavala's immediate release from pre-trial detention. Ankara did not comply. In his new complaint, the cultural patron refers to the period after the first 2019 ruling and is challenging his detention, the criminal proceedings initiated against him, and his conviction.

ECHR rulings are generally binding for Turkey as a member of the Council of Europe. After judges in Istanbul had decided that Kavala had to remain in pre-trial detention, the Council of Europe initiated infringement proceedings against Turkey. The Strasbourg organization, with 46 member states, monitors human rights compliance and is not an EU institution. Turkey has been a member of the Council of Europe since 1950.

content.title: Turkey ordered to pay 7,500 euros in compensation

content.text: In another 2022 ruling, the ECHR ordered Turkey to pay a fine for disregarding the 2019 decision. Turkey therefore had to pay 7,500 euros to Kavala. According to his own statements, the imprisoned activist refused Turkey's payment in protest.

Kavala had founded the cultural institute Anadolu Kültür, which also collaborates with several German institutions such as the Goethe-Institut in Istanbul. In 2023, the activist was awarded the prestigious Vaclav Havel Prize of the Council of Europe, which honors commitment to human rights.

content.title: Hope is fading for prisoners in Turkey

teaserImage.teaserCaption: Thousands of political prisoners had been counting on an opposition victory in the presidential and parliamentary elections. The opposition had promised a return to the rule of law.

content.title: The proceedings against Osman Kavala are a bitter farce

teaserImage.teaserCaption: The new arrest warrant issued against the cultural patron and businessman just hours after his acquittal in the Gezi Park trial is an absurd culmination of a scandalous proceeding. It clearly demonstrates how broken the Turkish justice system is.

metadata.nzzSummaryEN:
- The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) condemned Turkey for the detention and treatment of human rights activist Osman Kavala, declaring his life sentence based on disputed charges against free speech invalid.
- Turkey has repeatedly been urged to release Kavala but has ignored binding rulings, prompting the Council of Europe to initiate infringement proceedings.
- Kavala, awarded the Vaclav Havel Prize in 2023, protested against Turkey's fine and remains in detention.
metadata.nzzSummaryDE:
- The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) condemned Turkey for the detention and treatment of human rights activist Osman Kavala, whose life sentence was overturned on controversial charges against freedom of expression.
 Turkey has been repeatedly called upon to release Kavala, but has ignored the binding judgments. This has led to infringement proceedings against Turkey by the Council of Europe.
 Kavala, who received the Vaclav Havel Prize in 2023, protested the Turkish fine and remains imprisoned.
